title: Triangular faces of cis and mer octahedral complexes carrying one N and two Cl
summary: Type the composition of each coordination sphere into the panel, press Run experiment, and watch a model octahedron get built, its six numbered sites loaded with N and Cl donors, and each of its eight triangles turned towards you in turn while an inspector tallies the ones matching the pattern - the answer is the tally at the end, and it blinks when it lands.
subject: Chemistry
subtopics: Geometry of the octahedron: vertices, edges and faces
cis and trans isomers of an MA4B2 complex
fac and mer isomers of an MA3B3 complex
Counting faces by their corner composition
concepts: Only what is inside the square brackets is bonded to the metal - the chloride written outside is the counter-ion and never reaches a vertex
The six sites are numbered the usual way - 1, 2, 3, 4 round the square plane and 5, 6 axial - so the opposite (trans) pairs are 1-3, 2-4 and 5-6 and every other pair is cis
An octahedron has 6 vertices, 12 edges and 8 triangular faces, and every face takes exactly one vertex from each opposite pair
cis means 90 degrees apart, so two cis donors share an edge; trans means opposite, so no face contains both
fac means three mutually cis donors, which form one whole face; mer means one pair is trans and the third is cis to both
Every edge of an octahedron lies in exactly two faces, so a Cl-Cl edge contributes two faces carrying two chlorides
A count like this depends only on the isomer label, not on which particular vertices are drawn
formulas: faces = 2 x 2 x 2 = 8, one vertex from each opposite pair
each edge is shared by exactly 2 faces
cis-MA4B2: 1 B-B edge -> 2 faces with 1 A and 2 B
mer-MA3B3: 2 B-B edges -> 4 faces with 1 A and 2 B
fac-MA3B3: 3 B-B edges but one all-B face -> 3 faces with 1 A and 2 B

methods: Derived from first principles before any published solution was consulted: the eight faces, both isomer geometries and both counts were enumerated independently

The faces enumerated two ways: taking one vertex from each opposite pair gives 8, and brute force over all C(6,3) = 20 triples with the opposite-pair triples discarded gives the same 8. Euler's formula, 6 - 12 + 8 = 2, agrees

Exhaustive over placements rather than one drawing: all 15 ways of seating two chlorides were classified (12 cis, 3 trans) and every cis placement gives exactly 2 matching faces, every trans placement 0; all 20 ways of seating three were classified (8 fac, 12 mer) and every mer placement gives exactly 4, every fac placement 3. The answer therefore cannot depend on which vertices are drawn, and the page reproduces that table live
The face census closes: cis splits its eight faces 2/4/2/0 across 0, 1, 2 and 3 chlorides and mer splits them 0/4/4/0, both summing to 8, so no face is double-counted or missed
Structural cross-check by a different argument: a face carrying two chlorides is exactly a Cl-Cl edge, and every edge lies in two faces - cis has one such edge giving 2, mer has two giving 4

The distractors reproduced deliberately: fac instead of mer gives 2 + 3 = 5; trans instead of cis gives 0 + 4 = 4; counting 2 N + 1 Cl instead gives 4 + 4 = 8; putting the ionic chloride on a vertex needs seven vertices and is impossible. None is 6

Answer cross-checked afterwards against a published worked solution for this paper, which argues from the same Cl-Cl edges and reports the same 6. IIT Roorkee's official key was not retrievable at the time of writing

Headless-browser run of the finished page: 133 assertions driving the whole flow - the geometry the page is built on including the 1-to-6 site numbering and its trans pairs 1-3, 2-4, 5-6, the exhaustive placement check, the empty instrument panel with the answer nowhere on it, the refusal of seven donor atoms and of a face pattern that does not add to three, the isomer control adapting to the numbers typed and defining the isomer it is given along with the sites it seats, each of the six run steps in turn, pause and resume genuinely freezing and restarting the clock, the model turning to the face under inspection, the ledger and chips filling live in position numbers, the answer blinking on arrival and the blink stopping rather than looping, the result panel and the gate, browsing either complex afterwards and clicking a ledger row to re-inspect a face, all three traps reproduced as runs, theme toggle, clean console, zero horizontal overflow at 390 px and 360 px, and a bench that fits in one window
verification.note: IIT Roorkee's official key was not retrievable; the published solution used for cross-checking is a coaching-institute solution that argues from the same Cl-Cl edges and agrees on both intermediate counts, not only on the final number. Revision 2 renamed the six sites from axis labels to the conventional numbering 1 to 6, made the page define cis, trans, fac and mer and say which sites each one uses and why, and made the answer blink when it is produced. The chemistry and the answer are unchanged.

interactivity: Enter the data, run the experiment, watch it produce the answer: an instrument panel you fill in, a six-step inspection you watch, and a tally read off the finished run
One input for every quantity the question gives: the N and Cl donor counts of each coordination sphere, the isomer of each, and the composition of the face being looked for

The six sites are numbered 1 to 6 the way an octahedral complex normally is - 1, 2, 3, 4 round the square plane and 5, 6 axial - and the numbering key, with the trans pairs 1-3, 2-4 and 5-6, is printed under the model; every number appears on its own site and brightens on the face under inspection

The isomer control relabels itself from the numbers typed - two of one ligand offers cis / trans, three offers fac / mer, anything else says there is only one arrangement - and nothing is pre-selected, so the isomer is data the student supplies

Choosing an isomer makes the panel define it and say where it seats the ligands and why: cis is 90 degrees apart so the bench uses 1 and 5, one in the plane and one axial; mer has one trans pair and a third cis to both, so it uses 5, 6 and 1; trans uses the opposite pair 5 and 6; fac uses the mutually cis 1, 2 and 5

The bench refuses what it cannot build and says why: seven donor atoms will not fit on six vertices, which is exactly the counter-ion trap the question sets, and a face pattern that does not add to three is rejected against the field
A ghost octahedron idles on the bench before the run, so the apparatus is visibly waiting for data
Step 1 draws the cage in edge by edge and states why there are eight faces
Step 2 flies the ligands in to the vertices the isomer demands, and the Cl-Cl edges light up in orange as they land

Step 3 turns the model so each of the eight triangular faces points at the viewer in turn, shades the face under inspection, and reads its three corners out - the inspection is a physical action, not a table
Step 4 lifts the ligands off and lands the second complex on the same cage, so it is visibly the same eight faces with different labels
A live tally under the model counts the matching faces as they are found, with eight chips ticking off face by face
A face ledger fills in row by row with each face's corners, what sits on them in colour, and whether it matched
Six live gauges that fill in only as the run establishes them, with the total staying blank until the inspection starts
The working writes itself one line per step and the box scrolls itself to the newest line
Playback controls: pause, resume, replay and 0.5x / 1x / 2x speed, plus a change-the-data button that returns to the panel with the entries kept
After the run either complex can be reloaded onto the model, and clicking any ledger row turns the model to that face so it can be checked by eye

An exhaustive symmetry panel that lists every placement of the same isomer class - all 12 cis, all 12 mer - with the count each gives, proving that the vertices the bench chose could not have mattered
All three distractors are reachable as runs rather than warnings: fac gives 5, trans gives 4, and asking for 2 N + 1 Cl gives 8
A log of every run made, a lab notebook that writes itself, a record of the run that fills in quantity by quantity, and the derivation gated until an inspection finishes
Step-by-step solution with an independent verification log

When the tally lands, the answer blinks - in the result box, the header, the live tally and the total gauge - and the result box pulses a ring, so the moment it is produced is unmissable; the animation runs twice and stops rather than looping, and is suppressed for readers who ask for reduced motion
